rūpādijñānaṃ kartṛ kalpayatīti saṃbandhaḥ | nanu indriyavadeva tarhi kāraṇamātraṃ tat kiṃcit syāt; nīlaṃ, pītamityādi tu kutaḥ | atra ucyate kevalam iti | jñānākāraviṣayā yā pratyakṣapratītiḥ, tasyā yā pariniṣṭhā paśyāmītyadhyavasāyarūpā tasyā aviṣayatvena tadapi avaseyatvena kalpyate, natu kāraṇamātratayā yato'rthatvena ayamiti tatra adhyavasāyaḥ | kāraṇamātrānumānāt viśeṣaṃ darśayitumāha nahi iti | indriyajanitānāṃ jñānānāṃ pratyakṣasaṃvedanarūpāṇāṃ satyamindriyaṃ kāraṇaṃ, natu viṣayastairjñānena indriyaṃ paśyāmītyadhyavasāyasya ajananāt | indriyaṃ hi anumānasyaiva viṣayastadadhyavasāyenaiva adhyavasitatvāt, anumānaṃ ca viṣayo yasya ananyatrabhāvo viṣayārthaḥ | iha punaḥ iti prakṛte viśeṣamāha | agṛhītaḥ kathaṃ dṛṣṭatvena avasita iti cedāha sārūpyāt iti, yāvat kiṃcit deśakālasahacāri svarūpavaicitryaṃ jñānāntavṛttenīrlasya, tāvat sarvamavikalaṃ tadarpakasyeti sāmānābhihāramelananyāyena jñānīyākāraviṣayo'dhyavasāya utpannaḥ sārūpyakṛtāt vibhramāt jñānabhinnamarthākāramidantocitamadhyavasyāmi,- ityevamupajāyate, na (page 91) ca asau vibhramajo'pi adhyavasāyo gṛhītāyāṃ śuktikāyāṃ rupyāvasāya iva gṛhīte jñānākāre bāhye avasāyatayā bhramamātrasvabhāvaḥ, kintu arthapratibandhanāt maulikaṃ jñānākārārpaṇasamarthamarthaṃ kāraṇabhūtamadhyavasyan bhrāntirapi saṃbandhaḥ pramā iti nyāyena pramāṇavyāpāratāmātmani ādarśayati | yadāha arthasyāsaṃbhave'bhāvātpratyakṣe'pi pramāṇatā | pratibaddhasvabhāvasya taddhetutve samaṃ dvayam || iti | pramāṇavyāpāraśca ayaṃ bhavan darśanabalāt paśyāmītyevaṃ pratyakṣādinā adhyavasāyarūpatāṃ gṛhṇan pratyakṣamanugrāhakamarthasya amātya iva paravaśīkṛtaṃ rājānaṃ grāhakatvena vyavaharati, tataḥ pratyakṣagṛhīta eva bāhyo'rtha iti laukikamanusṛtaṃ bhavati | tarhi anumānasya kutra vyāpāraḥ | āha sasaṃvāda iti mūlakāraṇabhūtaḥ samarpaka ākārāṇāmasti arthastadākārasadṛśa iti | etāvati vyāpāro'numānasya | yaditu anumānaṃ tamarthaṃ bāhyamadhyavasīyamānaṃ bādheta sthairyamiva sattvahetuḥ, tadasau bāhyatādhyavasāyo nirmūla
**How the external object is inferred and confirmed** The Vijñānavādin grants that the cognition is self-luminous, but he presses on its inner form. "The cognition's blue-form," he says, "is a reflection (pratibimba); and a reflection demands a ground that produces it (the arpaka). So the external object is inferred." But then the classic objection follows: how can you infer an external object that is never perceived? An inference rests on a pervasion grasped in perception — and the external is never perceived at all. Abhinavagupta answers with the sense-organ analogy. The sense-organ itself is never perceived — yet we infer it as the cause of the perceptions it produces. The eye is inferred from the seeing, not seen. So too the external object: though never perceived as an object, it is inferred as the cause of its cognition. And the mechanism is the sārūpya, the conformity: the inner blue-form, with all its place-and-time variety, un-lost, points to its ground — the object similar to it. The determination "I see this object" arises from this conformity, and it is not a bare error, like the shell-silver in the grasped shell. For here is the crucial point, and Abhinavagupta states it boldly: even this determination, though it begins as error — the drawing of the inner form outward — is, by its bond to the thing, a *valid means*. As the rule has it, "even the error, being a relation, is a pramā." The determination, by the strength of the seeing, takes the form "I see" and enlists the perception as the object's helper — as a minister moves a king who has been won over. So the external object, thus determined and confirmed, is perceived (pratyakṣa-gṛhīta). And what, then, is the inference's own work? It is the sasaṃvāda — the agreement. The inference establishes that the root-cause, the ground of the forms (the arpaka), is the object similar to the form. This is its operation: not to create the object, but to confirm that the ground of the cognition's form is the thing, the similar thing, which the determination had already perceived. And if the inference were to work the other way — to refute the external, as the reasoning from momentariness refutes stability — then the whole determination of the external would be uprooted, and the practical dealings of the world would fail. If it did not determine at all, the dealing would likewise fail. So the external object, perceived and confirmed by the agreement, stands: it is real, and the cognition of it, with the perception as its helper and the inference as its confirmation, is a valid means. The upshot is a balanced realism. The object is not a bare thing hidden beyond all cognition; it is the ground of the cognition's form, inferred like the sense-organ and confirmed by the agreement. The determination "I see the jar" is not a fiction — it is a valid means, because it is bound to the thing and confirmed by the agreement. The external object is real, and the way we know it — perception and inference together — is sound. ---

> The jñānaśakti (the knowledge-power) is the capacity by which anything is known. Its central claim: > the manifestation is the very form of the objects. Their being *is* their being-manifested; to know a > thing is to be the light in which it appears. The Vijñānavādin agrees the object is not outside but > draws the wrong conclusion (no object at all). Abhinava replies: the inner blue-form is a reflection, > and a reflection expects a ground — so the object is real as the ground of the manifestation. > > The essence of the manifestation is the reflexive-awareness: the light that knows itself in knowing > the object. (reflection / ground).
